title: HE VIOLATED HER… THEN CALLED IT LOVE. BUT GOD NEVER CONFUSED LOVE WITH ABUSE.
paragraphs: HE VIOLATED HER… THEN CALLED IT LOVE. BUT GOD NEVER CONFUSED LOVE WITH ABUSE.

He wanted to marry the woman he had sexually violated. Her brothers wanted revenge. And somewhere between a man's obsession and a family's outrage was a wounded woman whose voice Scripture never records.
“A MAN FELL IN LOVE WITH THE WOMAN HE HAD SEXUALLY VIOLATED AND ASKED HIS FATHER TO ARRANGE THEIR MARRIAGE.” — Genesis 34:1–4
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
And then there are passages that make you close your Bible for a moment, stare into the distance, and wonder how human beings could become so cruel.
Genesis 34 is one of them.
No romantic music.
No beautiful wedding.
No fairy-tale ending.
Just a young woman named Dinah, a powerful man named Shechem, a devastating violation, and a disturbing declaration of love that came after the damage had already been done.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this story is that, thousands of years later, humanity is still confusing possession with affection, obsession with devotion, and apologies with genuine repentance.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Someone hurt you and then told you they loved you.
Someone destroyed your peace and then asked you to stay.
Someone wounded you deeply and expected their affection to erase everything they had done.
Perhaps they even used God, marriage, forgiveness, and Scripture to convince you that walking away would make you the sinful one.
But before we go any further, understand something.
Love does not become holy simply because the person who hurt you claims to feel it.
And marriage does not turn abuse into righteousness.
Dinah was the daughter of Jacob and Leah. Genesis 34:1 tells us that she went out to see the daughters of the land.
The Bible does not condemn her for going out.
It does not accuse her of dressing improperly.
It does not suggest that she invited what happened next.
Shechem, the son of Hamor, a prominent ruler of the region, saw her.
Then Scripture records something horrifying.
“And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her.”
— Genesis 34:2, KJV
The original Hebrew makes this passage especially disturbing.
וַיִּקַּח אֹתָהּ וַיִּשְׁכַּב אֹתָהּ וַיְעַנֶּהָ
Vayyiqqaḥ otah, vayyishkav otah, vaye‘anneha.
He took her, lay with her, and violated or humiliated her.
The final Hebrew verb, וַיְעַנֶּהָ — vaye‘anneha, comes from the root ענה (‘anah), which, in this grammatical form and context, conveys affliction, humiliation, or violation.
The same root appears in other biblical accounts involving sexual violence, including the devastating story of Tamar in 2 Samuel 13:14.
This is not presented as an innocent encounter between two consenting lovers.
Genesis 34:7 explicitly describes Shechem's conduct as an outrage, something that ought not to have been done.
The responsibility belongs to Shechem.
Not Dinah.
Not her decision to leave home.
Not her appearance.
Not her silence.
And if someone has ever made you feel responsible for the evil another person chose to commit against you, please remember that distinction.
Another person's sin is not your shame to carry.
But what happened next makes this passage even more unsettling.
“And his soul clave unto Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the damsel, and spake kindly unto the damsel.”
— Genesis 34:3, KJV
The Hebrew reads:
וַתִּדְבַּק נַפְשׁוֹ בְּדִינָה
Vattidbaq nafsho be-Dinah.
His soul clung to Dinah.
The verb comes from דָּבַק — davaq, meaning to cling, cleave, or hold fast.
Interestingly, this same Hebrew root appears in Genesis 2:24, where a man is described as cleaving to his wife.
But the presence of the same word does not make Shechem's behavior righteous.
Context matters.
A word describing attachment does not automatically establish the moral goodness of that attachment.
Scripture also uses the Hebrew verb אָהַב — ahav, meaning to love, when describing Shechem's feelings toward Dinah.
The text acknowledges his affection without excusing his actions.
That distinction should shake us.
A person can experience powerful emotions and still behave wickedly.
A person can desire your presence while disregarding your dignity.
A person can speak tenderly while refusing to take responsibility for the wounds they caused.
The intensity of someone's feelings is not the measure of their righteousness.
Paul gives us a profoundly different picture of love in 1 Corinthians 13:5:
“[Charity] doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own.”
The original Greek includes the expression:
οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς — ou zētei ta heautēs.
Love does not seek its own interests.
Biblical love is not merely about what someone wants to receive from another human being.
It considers the other person's good.
It does not demand access to another person's body, affection, trust, or future.
Shechem wanted Dinah.
But wanting someone and loving someone rightly are not necessarily the same thing.
Then came his request.
“And Shechem spake unto his father Hamor, saying, Get me this damsel to wife.”
— Genesis 34:4, KJV
In Hebrew:
קַח־לִי אֶת־הַיַּלְדָּה הַזֹּאת לְאִשָּׁה
Qaḥ-li et-hayyaldah hazzot le’ishah.
Get this young woman for me as a wife.
Notice what the narrative records.
He wanted her.
He became attached to her.
He spoke tenderly to her.
He wanted to marry her.
But nowhere in Genesis 34 do we hear Shechem confess his wrongdoing, express remorse, or ask Dinah for forgiveness.
We are not told what Dinah wanted.
We are not given her response.
We are not allowed to hear her thoughts.
And we must resist the temptation to invent them.
Her silence in the narrative is not evidence of consent.
Shechem's desire for marriage is not evidence of repentance.
His willingness to pay a substantial bride-price later in the chapter is not evidence that the violation had been healed.
You cannot purchase forgiveness, negotiate away another person's wounds, or turn wrongdoing into righteousness through a wedding ceremony.
How many people today are still trapped inside that misunderstanding?
The husband who believes buying flowers erases his cruelty.
The partner who thinks saying “I love you” cancels repeated betrayal.
The religious leader who demands forgiveness without accepting accountability.
The person who cries when confronted, not necessarily because they understand the damage they caused, but because they fear losing the relationship.
Tears can accompany repentance.
But tears alone are not repentance.
Promises can accompany transformation.
But promises alone are not transformation.
John the Baptist declared:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
— Matthew 3:8, KJV
The Greek word for repentance, μετάνοια — metanoia, describes a change of mind and heart that, in its biblical context, calls a person to turn from sin toward God.
Genuine repentance produces fruit.
It accepts responsibility.
It abandons excuses.
It respects boundaries.
It does not demand that the wounded person immediately restore what the offender destroyed.
And it does not treat forgiveness as permission to escape consequences.
You do not owe the internet your private story. But those few words can become a prayer for yourself and for someone silently reading beside you.
Because Genesis 34 does not end with Shechem's marriage proposal.
It becomes even darker.
Dinah's brothers were grieved and furious when they learned what had happened. Their anger at the violation was understandable.
But Simeon and Levi eventually responded through deception and deadly vengeance against the men of the city. The other sons of Jacob subsequently plundered it.
One terrible injustice became the occasion for further injustice.
And this is another uncomfortable truth Scripture refuses to hide.
Being wronged does not make every response righteous.
Pain does not sanctify cruelty.
Anger at evil does not give us unlimited permission to commit evil ourselves.
Jacob would later condemn the violence of Simeon and Levi in Genesis 49:5–7.
The Bible does not require us to choose between excusing Shechem's violation and celebrating the brothers' vengeance.
Both can be condemned.
God's justice is not indifference toward evil, nor is it uncontrolled human revenge.
Romans 12:19 reminds believers that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

That does not mean victims must remain silent, refuse legal protection, or abandon the pursuit of justice. Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining wrongdoing.
Seeking safety is not revenge.
Reporting abuse is not bitterness.
Establishing boundaries is not rebellion against God.
And refusing to return to an unsafe relationship is not necessarily a failure to forgive.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, and restored trust are related, but they are not interchangeable.
Reconciliation cannot be manufactured by demanding that a wounded person pretend nothing happened.
Trust cannot be commanded into existence.
And grace must never become a religious weapon used to protect an offender from accountability.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about Genesis 34 is how much everyone else gets to speak.
Shechem speaks.
Hamor speaks.
Jacob speaks.
Dinah's brothers speak.
Men negotiate.
Men make decisions.
Men become angry.
Men discuss marriage, wealth, honor, and revenge.
Yet Dinah's own words are never recorded.
We cannot know everything she experienced.
But we can recognize how easily the wounded become overshadowed when everyone else becomes more concerned with their own interests.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still feels painfully modern.
Sometimes people care more about protecting the family's reputation than protecting the wounded person.
Sometimes churches fear scandal more than they fear the sin behind it.
Sometimes communities ask survivors to remain quiet because the truth would make powerful people uncomfortable.
Sometimes the person who speaks about the wound is treated as a greater problem than the person who inflicted it.
But darkness does not become righteousness simply because it has been concealed.
Ephesians 5:11 says:
“And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.”
The Gospel does not need lies to protect its reputation.
Jesus Christ is the truth.
And the truth does not become an enemy of the Church when it exposes wrongdoing within the Church.
This is where the story must lead us beyond Shechem, beyond Dinah's brothers, and beyond the brokenness of Jacob's household.
It must lead us to Jesus.

Centuries later, Jesus would stand before a crowd of religious accusers with a woman caught in adultery in John 8:1–11, a passage whose manuscript history is debated but whose themes of mercy and repentance are consistent with Christ's teaching elsewhere in Scripture.
Throughout the Gospels, Jesus consistently demonstrates compassion toward the vulnerable while confronting hypocrisy and sin.
He does not confuse mercy with moral indifference.
He does not confuse authority with entitlement.
He does not confuse love with domination.
Consider how radically different Christ's love is from the possessiveness we encounter in Genesis 34.
Shechem took.
Jesus gave Himself.
Shechem pursued what he wanted.
Jesus surrendered Himself for the good of those He came to save.
Jesus said:
“Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
— John 15:13, KJV
The Greek word translated as love here is ἀγάπη — agapē.
The word itself is not a magical guarantee of righteousness; its meaning is shaped by context. And in this passage, Jesus defines the greatness of love through self-sacrifice.
At Calvary, Christ did not demonstrate love by demanding that others bleed for His desires.
He gave His own life.
He bore our sins.
He endured suffering.
He died and rose again so that sinners could receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life through faith in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not a sentimental message that evil does not matter.
Not a religious excuse to continue hurting people.
Not a promise that every broken relationship must be restored.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable depth of divine grace.
And that grace reaches people on both sides of human brokenness.
To the person who has been violated, hear this carefully.
You are not morally stained by another person's decision to sin against you.
Your dignity is not determined by what someone did to your body.
Your worth is not diminished because someone disregarded it.
You do not need to marry, reconcile with, or return to the person who harmed you to prove your devotion to Jesus.
You are a human being made in the image of God.
And the Lord is not indifferent to your suffering.
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.”
— Psalm 34:18, KJV
Healing may take time.
It may involve counseling, medical care, legal protection, trusted relationships, prayer, and difficult conversations.
There is no spiritual failure in seeking appropriate help.
And to the person who recognizes something of Shechem in their own behavior, there is a different message.
Stop hiding behind your feelings.
Stop calling your entitlement love.
Stop demanding forgiveness from the person you wounded.
Stop using grace as a shelter for unrepentant sin.
Come before Jesus Christ without excuses.
Confess what you have done.
Accept accountability and lawful consequences.
Respect the boundaries of those you have harmed.
Seek genuine transformation.
The Gospel offers forgiveness even to grievous sinners who turn to Christ. But receiving God's forgiveness does not entitle anyone to renewed access to the person they hurt.
Zacchaeus demonstrated the fruit of repentance through his willingness to make restitution in Luke 19:8.
David, confronted with his sin, confessed in Psalm 51.
Paul taught that godly sorrow produces repentance in 2 Corinthians 7:10.
Grace is not God pretending that sin never happened.
Grace is God offering redemption through Jesus Christ to people who could never redeem themselves.
And transformation means we cannot remain comfortable with the very darkness from which Christ calls us.
This is what we mean when we say:
Jesus does not rewrite evil into innocence.
He does not rewrite abuse into romance.
He does not rewrite injustice into something the wounded should celebrate.
He redeems people.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
He restores dignity to those whom the world has treated as disposable.
He gives hope beyond the worst chapters of our lives.
And He promises a future in which suffering, mourning, and death will ultimately pass away (Revelation 21:4).
The scandal does not have to become your identity.
The wound does not have to define your entire future.
The person who hurt you does not get to determine your worth.
And the sin you have committed does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's forgiveness when you genuinely turn to Him.
But never mistake redemption for denial.
Jesus is not asking us to pretend the darkness was beautiful.
He is calling us into His marvelous light.
There may come a day when you need these Scriptures again.
Let that declaration remind others that compassion for the wounded and accountability for wrongdoing are not enemies of the Gospel.
We want to reach people who may never enter a church building but might encounter the truth of Jesus through something you share.

Scripture encourages believers to support those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). It also teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not from guilt or compulsion.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You are not purchasing God's favor.
You are not buying salvation.
You are helping make biblical teaching available to others.
Become part of a community committed to biblical truth, spiritual growth, repentance, healing, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Never underestimate what God can accomplish through a willing heart.

And tonight, when the world becomes quiet and the memories become loud, remember what Genesis 34 teaches us about the darkness of human sin and what Calvary reveals about the greatness of divine love.
What happened to Dinah should never be romanticized.
What happened to you should never be minimized.
What you have done wrong should never be justified.
But none of us should underestimate what Jesus Christ can accomplish through His truth, justice, mercy, and redeeming grace.
The hands that wounded you do not have the final authority over your story. Your Creator does—and His hands bear the scars of a love that gave itself rather than taking from you.
